court-45.claim: The Delhi High Court closed a petition by two electors whose names were left off Delhi's roll after they moved house and could not fill the enumeration form. They had asked the Court to quash para 4(c) of the SIR guidelines and to change the procedure that requires such electors to seek fresh inclusion through Form 6, and to restore their entries and let them move them to their new address through Form 8. The Commission's standing counsel said they could file Form 6 and that the Electoral Registration Officer would help. The first petitioner said that filing Form 6 would be a false declaration. The bench said that, since the suggestion came from the Commission's counsel on the officer's instructions, his fear of being accused of a false declaration was misplaced. It closed the petition and said the petitioners could file Form 6 if they wished, to be processed in accordance with law. It did not decide the challenge to the guidelines.

court-58.claim: In Hemtabad, a seat reserved for Scheduled Castes in Uttar Dinajpur district, the Election Commission has filed appeals against 15,381 of the 34,327 electors whom judicial officers examined and found eligible, 44.8%, The Wire reported. Of the 13,776 pending appeals, 12,758 carry the code that activists read, and The Wire says it verified, as the batch lodged on the evening of 5 April 2026, 978 carry the code for 6 April, and 40 were filed online. The paper reported that 599 of the appeals with the 5 April code concern electors cleared in the constituency's twelfth and last supplementary list, which was published on 6 April, so the appeals were on record before the list that cleared those electors was made public. The 599 come from nine polling stations, and 162 of them from part 237. Of the 2,65,162 electors on Hemtabad's draft roll, 52,542 were placed under adjudication, and judicial officers struck 18,215 off the roll and found 34,327 eligible. By The Wire's classification of names, which counts the elector's own name or a relative's, at least 97.7% of the electors appealed against have Muslim names, as do all 599, and at least 97% of all those the judges cleared do, so the appeals largely mirror who was cleared. court-65.claim: The Wire's classification of the names in appeal records compiled by the Civic Research Group finds that at least 14,39,797 of the 16,08,175 electors against whose inclusion the Election Commission has appealed, after judicial officers examined them and found them eligible, have Muslim names, 89.5%. In every group the Commission appealed against between 46.5% and 51.2% of the electors the judges cleared, and the report says that across seats there is almost no relationship between a seat's Muslim share and the share of its cleared electors appealed against. It counts 137 constituencies where at least 90% of the electors appealed against have Muslim names, and 2,62,416 electors with Muslim names facing appeals in the 160 seats where Muslims are under a fifth of the population. court-66.claim: Residents of Maharashtra filed a writ petition before the Kolhapur Bench of the Bombay High Court through the advocate Asim Sarode asking it to quash 14 administrative orders passed by the Election Commission and the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over the past ten months, Bar and Bench reported on 24 September. The petition relies on The Indian Express's report that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi objected to these decisions on at least 14 occasions, and says the objections concerned voter registration, deletion and restoration of names, the electoral roll database, the functioning of registration officers and software. It argues that the Commission did not act in accordance with section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, and that the Chief Election Commissioner failed to discharge his duties faithfully, so that no protection can extend to his actions in office. It also challenges the changes made to Form 6 in July. It asks for the 14 orders to be quashed, for the revision in Maharashtra to be stayed, for every elector deleted in Maharashtra in the revision to be restored, for the Assembly elections due in the states where the revision was held to be postponed until rolls are prepared in accordance with law, and for a judicial committee headed by a retired High Court judge to inquire into the deletions and the blockages in the software. On 28 September a bench of Justices Sharmila Deshmukh and Neeraj Dhote declined Sarode's request to hear it that day or the next and listed it for 22 October, Bar and Bench reported. The bench asked what was urgent about it and what private right the petitioners held against the Commission, and Sarode replied that the petition was filed for voters who feel their rights are being infringed. No report of a hearing on 22 October or of any later order was found.

court-69.claim: The First Additional Sessions Judge, Sujit Kumar, on 30 October rejected the Banbhoolpura police's application to stay a Haldwani magistrate's order of 6 October to register an FIR over Form 7s seeking the deletion of 28 electors (form7-36), Dainik Jagran and Live Hindustan reported on 11 November. The station house officer of Banbhoolpura had filed a revision petition against the order and asked for it to be stayed. The court held that the police are not a victim or an aggrieved party in the matter and that registering an FIR and investigating on information of a cognisable offence is their legal duty, Dainik Jagran reported. By the account of the complainant's advocate, Manish Kumar Pandey, the court also questioned why no FIR had been registered for about 24 days. The revision petition is listed for 7 December 2026, and with the stay refused the magistrate's order stands. The complainant, a resident of Indiranagar who says he is the BJP's booth level agent, alleges that an unknown person misused his identity and login to file the Form 7s online on 12 August 2026 against electors of part 134, that he learnt of it on 20 August, and that he neither filed them nor authorised anyone to. Live Hindustan reports that the order of 6 October was passed by the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Shubhangi Gupta. It also reports the complainant's account that he went to Delhi on 30 October and raised the case with more than 20 MPs and senior leaders of the INDIA bloc, among them Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi, P. Chidambaram, Mahua Moitra and Mehbooba Mufti.

Live Hindustan says the allegations have not been confirmed and that the investigation of the forms, user IDs and login records on the Commission's portal could show who filed them. court-73.claim: Karnataka's State Election Commission applied to the Supreme Court on 12 November for leave to hold the elections to the five city corporations under the Greater Bengaluru Authority on the final rolls published on 18 April 2026, and for time until 31 January 2027 to complete them on those earlier ward-wise rolls, Deccan Herald reported on 13 November. It also asked for leave to hold the elections to all panchayats and urban local bodies in the state on the Assembly rolls as they stood on 1 October 2025. The Supreme Court had directed on 17 July that the five corporation elections be completed by 31 December 2026. The State Election Commission told the Court that unforeseen delays in the final publication of the Assembly rolls on 27 October, and the Election Commission's not supplying complete and authenticated roll data since then, had disrupted its schedule. It said it needs the full data, with the additions, deletions, transpositions and corrections, to divide the rolls by ward and to map, verify and publish them. Deccan Herald reports that the data had still not been supplied when the application was filed. It estimated that if it had to wait for the new rolls it would need at least two months after receiving the data to prepare the ward rolls and another month to hold the elections. It said it had already prepared and published rolls for the five corporations from the data of 1 October 2025 that the Election Commission had supplied, and had printed and distributed state voter identity cards on that basis. On 5 November it had told the five corporations to prepare ward rolls from the final rolls of 27 October (protest-66).

court-75.claim: The office of West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer told the Registrar General of the Calcutta High Court in memos dated 12 October and 29 October 2026 that judicial officers had not decided 815 adjudication cases and had decided 5,004 more without e-signing them, The Wire reported on 13 November. It says the Commission's IT team wrote on 6 August that the logins of the judicial officers of the constituencies concerned had been reactivated, and it asks the Registrar General to have those officers e-sign the decided cases and decide the rest at the earliest. It refers to an earlier memo of 7 August. The Wire reports that the memo of 29 October gives the same two figures, and that the office asked district election officers the same day to report on these cases by 3 November, before the integrated draft roll of the special summary revision due on 23 November. The Wire says the Commission's ECINET report 'Individuals Under Adjudication' of 9 April, which it has seen, records 22,163 cases that judges had not decided when the judicial review ended and 83,504 that they had decided and not signed, 44,027 of them found eligible. It reports that 12,337 of the undecided cases were in Murshidabad, 5,194 in Purba Bardhaman and 3,374 in South 24 Parganas, across 67 constituencies, with 3,183 in Farakka. The Wire's own count, from the rolls of 304 polling stations in 11 of Murshidabad's 22 constituencies, is 29,347 electors still marked under adjudication, which it says is five times the number the Chief Electoral Officer's office gives for the whole state. In three polling stations of Mahadebnagar gram panchayat in Farakka, whose roll as revised up to 6 April it has seen, it counts 1,914, and booth level officers told it that the judicial review there never took place. The Wire says an elector whose case was never decided has no order to take to the appellate tribunals and was not able to vote in April.

court-76.claim: The Election Commission filed a supplementary affidavit in the Supreme Court on 14 November 2026, The Hindu reported. LiveLaw reports that Deputy Election Commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu filed it on behalf of the Commission in the writ petition that leads the batch on the Commission's functioning, W.P.(C) No. 1246 of 2026 (court-52, court-53). The interrogatories that INDIA bloc leaders asked the Court on 16 November for leave to serve also describe it as sworn by Yeturu (court-78). The Indian Express describes it as a joint affidavit of the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and the Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi. The Hindu gives no case number and reports the affidavit together with the concerns about Form 6 raised by the petitioners in the case on Delhi's revision, in which Anjali Bhardwaj is a petitioner (court-54, court-60, court-61). The affidavit says the Commission took note of the Court's suggestion at the hearing of 28 October that it reach out to electors left off as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate, and that by a communication of 6 November it directed the Chief Electoral Officers of the states and union territories where the revision is under way, which LiveLaw lists as Delhi, Maharashtra, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana and Nagaland, to let electors left off the draft roll submit the enumeration form (Annexure A) to the Electoral Registration Officer or Assistant Electoral Registration Officer for their current ordinary residence. An elector who has not shifted may submit the signed form with an Annexure B statement giving the reason it was not submitted earlier, in person or through family members, to the Electoral Registration Officer, the Assistant Electoral Registration Officer or the booth level officer, and that an option to submit it online with e-sign will be available on ECINET. An elector who has shifted within the state does not need Form 8 and may submit the enumeration form with an Annexure C statement giving the new address and Assembly constituency, and proof of address, to the Electoral Registration Officer or Assistant Electoral Registration Officer of the new constituency. The affidavit says booth-wise lists of electors marked absent, shifted, dead or duplicate are to be displayed afresh with the probable reasons why they were not included, and that Electoral Registration Officers are to process the enumeration forms of these electors under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 and re-assign the same EPIC number to them. It says a previously enrolled elector who has already filed Form 6 need not submit the enumeration form again, and that such applications will be processed under the clarification of 3 November (court-60). It repeats that clarification, that no prosecution will be launched against anyone for filing Form 6 merely because the applicant was enrolled before the revision and was not in the draft roll, provided the applicant is not enrolled in any other Parliamentary or Assembly constituency and the declaration is otherwise in accordance with law. ThePrint, carrying a PTI report, also reported the affidavit and says the Chief Electoral Officers have been asked to give the clarification wide publicity, in local languages as well. The affidavit says a mechanism has been directed to ensure that no eligible elector is deprived of the chance to be included in the final roll, with due care to avoid duplicate enrolment. It also says that after a new Deputy Election Commissioner joined on 2 November, a work order of 4 November gave oversight of the Commission's IT division to a Senior Deputy Election Commissioner, that the Director General (IT) puts the division's files to the Commission through that officer, and that the IT division has always been under the supervision of a Deputy Election Commissioner. The Times of India also reported the affidavit, from PTI. The batch on the Commission's functioning was tentatively listed for 17 November (court-53), and the Delhi case is listed for 19 November (court-61).

court-78.claim: INDIA bloc leaders asked the Supreme Court on 16 November 2026 for permission to put 48 written questions, known as interrogatories, to the Election Commission, Business Standard reported. The Congress announced the application in a post on X and published with it 17 pages of the filing, headed Annexure A-1, Interrogatories on behalf of the Petitioners. The filing names who is to answer each question on affidavit. They are Deputy Election Commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu, whom it describes as the deponent of the Commission's counter affidavit of 26 October (court-52) and of its supplementary affidavit of 14 November (court-76), the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and the Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, who are to answer from their own knowledge, including their own approval, participation, objection, dissent or concurrence, and the Commission's Director General (IT). Where a question is put to more than one person, each is to answer it on a separate affidavit. The questions are grouped in ten parts. They ask on what date and by what means each of the three Commissioners approved the filing of the counter affidavit, and in which file and on what date the Commission took the decision, recited in its order of 24 June 2025, to begin the revision in the entire country. They ask whether the order of the Commission's first appellate authority in an RTI appeal, which said the Commission had so far taken no decision on a revision across the country in 2025, was correct when it was made. They ask on how many occasions between 19 February 2025 and 26 October 2026 Sandhu or Joshi recorded in writing an objection, dissent or reservation on the revision, ECINET, Form 6 or the filing of appeals, and whether any decision on the revision was taken by majority under Section 18(2) of the 2023 Act. court-79.claim: Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders have told the Supreme Court in a rejoinder to the Election Commission's counter affidavit of 26 October (court-52) that the Commission gave no proof of its claim that the SIR was a unanimous decision of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, The Wire reported on 16 November 2026. The rejoinder says the counter affidavit gives no particulars or dates of that approval, and that the Court should not take into account "a bare assertion of unanimous decision of the Election Commissioners without perusal of the relevant recorded files". It says the affidavit does not explain when the decision to hold the revision across the country was taken, where it was recorded, or how the Commission's RTI replies that no such decision had been taken are to be reconciled with its order of 24 June 2025. It says the affidavit was signed by a Deputy Election Commissioner on behalf of the three members, who are all senior to him, and that a general statement by an administrative officer cannot take the place of the primary records or of the members' own explanation. It says that Sandhu and Joshi writing to the Cabinet Secretary is "itself inconsistent with the picture of unanimous functioning" that the Commission presents. On Form 6 it says that calling the declaration a separate component does not change the fact that an applicant using the online Form 6 process "was required to encounter and complete the additional declaration as part of that process". The Wire reports that the petitioners say 97 electors in Goa were deleted and could not be added back because local electoral officials could not get into the software to enrol them again, and that the Commission's affidavit said 88 were added back through Form 6 applications. Bar and Bench reported the same affidavit as saying 88 of the 97 had since applied through Form 6 (court-52). The rejoinder says the affidavit "does not deny that the software lacked a facility to restore these electors". It says the office order of 1997 on which the Commission relies does not cover the design of the roll software, changes to statutory forms or application procedures, or the bringing of litigation or appeals. On the appeals filed by officers of the West Bengal Chief Electoral Officer against electors the tribunals had cleared, it says that if they were acts of the Commission, "the respondents must disclose the decision of the commission authorising the same, together with the relevant approval and delegation records". The Hindu reported the same day that Rahul Gandhi had told the Court that the Commission produced no proof that the SIR was a unanimous decision of the three members, and that the Commission's affidavit of 26 October answered a petition by INDIA bloc leaders led by him. The Wire gives the hearing as 17 November before a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, and the Supreme Court's cause list for that day lists the petition as item 26.5 (court-78).

court-97.claim: The bench of the Chief Justice, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana said on 25 November 2026 that it was inclined to stay an order of a Calcutta High Court division bench that restrained West Bengal's State Election Commission from issuing a notification for the Kolkata Municipal Corporation elections until a single judge decides a challenge to the delimitation of the corporation's wards, PTI reported. The delimitation may raise the number of wards from 144 to 209. The bench said the writ petition before the single judge would be directed to be transferred to the division bench, which would pass a fresh order, and it asked the Solicitor General, Tushar Mehta, to seek instructions by 30 November. LawTrend reports that the bench also indicated that the elections could remain on hold until the division bench forms a view, and that the Court has not yet stayed the High Court's order. The petitioner in the High Court, Dipu Das, a former councillor of the CPI(M), alleged that the delimitation exercise was undertaken on the basis of electoral rolls instead of the actual population, and so left a substantial number of residents out of consideration. He asked the High Court to declare the whole exercise of fixing the number of wards void and to quash the gazette notification of 11 September expanding the wards. He also said the corporation had no elected council and that its former chairperson had been appointed its administrator after the House was dissolved on 8 June. The single judge refused an interim stay on 29 October and Das appealed to the division bench. PTI reports the division bench's order as saying that the state government could allow its chosen administrator to make a tailor-made recommendation and then be bound by it, in effect allowing the government to recommend amendments to itself, and that section 601 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act vests in the corporation the power to make a binding recommendation on the delimitation of its own wards. The order said its observations were tentative as far as the final disposal of the writ petition was concerned.
